extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in the Volkswagen emissions scandal and regulatory responses
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and document regulatory, legal, technical and consumer-remedy standards and expectations arising from an automotive emissions-standards scandal (Dieselgate). Useful for reporting, policy analysis, or regulatory compliance review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repairs must achieve legal EU emissions compliance without impairing engine performance or consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: According to VW, its proposed solutions will be designed to achieve legal EU emissions compliance without impairing engine performance or consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators (and public scrutiny) expect fixes to restore emissions conformity while preserving vehicle performance and fuel economy. However, multiple tests and recalls found software updates sometimes increased fuel consumption (e.g., Amarok +0.5 L/100 km) or reduced power output, and such side-effects can delay approval and rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall plan submission deadlines and approval by KBA
rubrics_metrics.description: KBA requires Volkswagen to send a recall plan to KBA before the end of October for 2.0‑litre cars, and end of November for 1.2 and 1.6‑litre cars; if KBA approves a plan, Volkswagen can then start handling the cars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National authorities may set specific, binding deadlines for submission of recall plans; meeting these procedural timelines is required before remediation work can begin in that jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: KBA requirement to remove defeat-device software and ensure emission rules are fulfilled
rubrics_metrics.description: The German authorities require that Volkswagen remove the software and that Volkswagen ensures that emission rules are fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators can mandate removal of non-compliant software and demand demonstrable conformity to emission limits as a condition of resolving a recall; technical fixes must be shown to bring vehicles into compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall plans must adequately address overall impacts on vehicle performance, emissions and safety (CARB standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: US regulators (CARB) rejected Volkswagen's recall plans for affected 2.0‑litre diesel engines, claiming that these 'do not adequately address overall impacts on vehicle performance, emissions and safety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory acceptance of a repair plan hinges not only on emissions reductions but also on ensuring the fix does not create safety problems or unacceptable changes to performance/fuel economy; plans must document and demonstrate acceptable overall impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement powers: quarantine, recall, sales bans and per-vehicle fines
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities can quarantine vehicles (EPA quarantined some 2016 models), recall vehicles, ban sales (Switzerland banned sales), and impose fines (e.g., EPA could seek fines up to US$37,500 per vehicle; EU fines up to €30,000 per car).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement tools vary by jurisdiction but typically include vehicle quarantines, mandatory recalls, sales bans, and significant per-vehicle monetary penalties; these are used to compel compliance and punish violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer remediation and compensation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation/remedy options used include vouchers, cash payments, buy-backs, repairs or replacement cars, and claims funds; US settlement included substantial compensation and buybacks of nearly 500,000 2.0‑litre vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory settlements and litigation can require manufacturers to offer multiple remedy paths (buyback, modification, or cash) and create claims funds or vouchers; settlements may differ across jurisdictions and be subject to court oversight or mediator negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with investigations and produce documents
rubrics_metrics.description: US officials criticized Volkswagen for citing German law to withhold documents and for slowness in producing US files; regulators expect timely, full cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During investigations, companies are expected to provide documents and cooperate promptly; invoking foreign law to withhold documents can draw regulatory criticism and impede negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for realistic, on-road emissions testing regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The European Parliament urged the bloc to establish authority to oversee car-emissions and called for tougher, more 'realistic' emissions tests (real-driving emissions) rather than lab-only cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One regulatory lesson from the scandal is that laboratory test cycles can be gamed; regulators increasingly demand real-world testing (RDE/PEMS) and institutional oversight to prevent manipulation and ensure conformity in real driving conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical fix requirements vary by engine model; hardware may be required
rubrics_metrics.description: It was unclear whether repairs would include hardware modifications such as selective catalytic reduction (SCR) upgrades; some engines (e.g., 1.6‑litre) required hardware changes while others (1.2 and 2.0‑litre) required only software updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators and manufacturers must identify which combinations of hardware and software changes are necessary per engine/type and justify the chosen remedy; complexity and time-to-fix vary accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to notify owners and offer rectification
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen Group vehicle drivers in the UK started receiving notification letters, to 'rectify the issue', and recalls were scheduled in waves with specified target dates by engine size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recall processes include formal notification to owners and a timeline for rectification; communication and logistics planning are expected parts of compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local legal requirements may cause rejection of recall plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen's recall plan for South Korea, submitted on 6 January 2016, was rejected by the authorities, as it failed to meet a number of key legal requirements; revised plan was also rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recall/repair plans must meet jurisdiction-specific legal and technical requirements; a plan acceptable in one market may be rejected elsewhere, requiring tailored submissions and possibly additional measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical fixes must be effective across operating conditions (e.g., ambient temperatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court ruled that updated software didn't properly address the emissions, citing a tested Tiguan turbodiesel engine that only reduced emissions in the ambient temperature range of 10–32 °C (50–90 °F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies must demonstrably reduce emissions across the full range of real-world operating conditions; partial effectiveness limited to narrow temperature ranges may be deemed insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification disclosure: vehicles/applications must disclose emissions-related software during certification
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, Volkswagen withdrew its application for emissions certification for its 2016 diesel models after regulators quarantined some models pending proof that their catalysts perform the same on the road as in tests; failure to disclose software that affects emissions led to investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers are required to disclose emissions-related software and configurations during type-approval/certification; nondisclosure can trigger investigations, quarantines and denial/withdrawal of certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal and civil accountability thresholds (prosecution and fines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple countries opened criminal investigations, prosecutors raided offices, executives were charged (e.g., Winterkorn), and courts imposed fines and sentences; examples include Germany's €1 billion fine for failing to monitor employees and Canada CA$196.5 million guilty plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory breaches can trigger both civil remedies (fines, settlements, consumer compensation) and criminal prosecutions against corporate officers; the nature and severity of accountability differ across jurisdictions but can include multi‑year prison sentences and large corporate fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory bodies can establish new powers and institutional oversight post-crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: In September 2020, EU laws changed and the European Commission gained the right to check car conformity to emission standards and to recall vehicles when needed, with fines up to €30,000 per car.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scandals can lead to legislative change strengthening regulatory oversight, new conformity-check powers, and higher penalties; compliance frameworks may be tightened accordingly.
